analysis.one_liner: Converts the largest state-chartered banks into national banks under a single federal regulator.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in July 2023, drew zero cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would automatically turn any state-chartered bank with at least $100 billion in assets into a national bank, supervised by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, within 180 days. Today those big banks are supervised by the Federal Reserve or the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, usually alongside a state regulator. The change would put them under the same single regulator that oversees national banks like the biggest Wall Street firms. It never went anywhere: no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest state-chartered banks would be converted by operation of law into national banks, ending split oversight by the Federal Reserve or the FDIC and by state regulators, and putting them solely under the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency [S2][S3]. A single regulator means one point of contact, one rulebook, and no divided supervision. Any benefit to depositors would come only if consolidated supervision turned out to be stronger than the current split system.

how_it_helps.text: State-chartered banks with average total assets of $100 billion or more would automatically become national banking associations 180 days after the quarter in which they crossed that threshold, supervised and regulated by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Under current law, banks of that size chartered by a state are instead regulated by the Federal Reserve or the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation; the bill removes that arrangement.
Converted banks keep the same powers, duties, and liabilities as banks originally organized as national banks, and may keep operating existing branches.

During the transition, the Comptroller may allow converted banks to keep holding activities and investments that do not conform to national bank requirements, and may extend or accelerate compliance dates based on effects on financial stability.

analysis.who_pays: The Federal Reserve and the FDIC would lose supervisory authority over the biggest state-chartered banks, and state regulators would lose their role entirely [S2][S3]. The converting banks would bear the cost of restructuring into a national charter and winding down or getting approval for activities that do not fit national bank rules [S3]. The broader public carries the risk if concentrating supervision of a dozen or so of the country's largest banks in one agency weakens oversight; bank failures land on the deposit insurance fund and the economy.

drawbacks.text: The bill consolidates supervision of the largest state-chartered banks into a single agency, the Comptroller of the Currency, ending divided oversight by the Federal Reserve or the FDIC and eliminating any state regulator's role in watching banks chartered in their states [S2][S3]. The Comptroller is funded by fees from the very banks it supervises, a structure widely criticized as creating an incentive toward leniency.

Conversion is automatic by operation of law with no application, hearing, or opt-out, and the Comptroller receives broad discretion to set compliance timing and to approve or deny banks' requests to keep nonconforming activities after conversion [S3].
The bill never received a hearing, so the case that one regulator would have prevented bank failures was never examined; it drew no cosponsors from either party [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill gestures at is real: the 2023 failures of Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank, both state-chartered, exposed gaps in how the Fed, the FDIC, and state regulators watched the largest banks. But the remedy as written is blunt. It automatically hands about a dozen of the biggest banks the charter and the single regulator (the OCC) that national banks have historically found most accommodating, strips state and other federal supervisors of any role, and gives the Comptroller wide discretion over timing and exceptions — all with no record of analysis, since the bill never got a hearing. Whatever its merit, it died with zero cosponsors, so the public debate never happened.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced in July 2023, the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. J.D. Vance introduced the Bank Failure Prevention Act in the Senate on July 26, 2023.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.

The bill would automatically convert state-chartered banks with $100 billion or more in assets into national banks overseen by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, replacing Federal Reserve or FDIC supervision.
No further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed. Large state-chartered banks keep their existing split supervision by the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, and state regulators, and no regulator gains or loses authority. Because the bill mainly would have reshaped the regulatory arrangement of the biggest banks, its quiet death largely leaves the banking industry where it was — while the underlying questions about how the largest banks are supervised were never taken up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — big banks keep existing regulators

for.name: Sen. J.D. Vance
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bank Failure Prevention Act on July 26, 2023.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (Chair Sherrod Brown)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill — no hearing or markup appears in its history — so it never advanced to the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and never came to a vote, so there is no record of where senators stood [S4].

industries.industry: Large state-chartered banks ($100B or more in assets)
industries.note: They would gain a single federal regulator (the Comptroller of the Currency) and end divided oversight, but give up state charter flexibility, bear conversion costs, and face national-bank restrictions on some activities [S3]. Their gain comes from choosing the charter and regulator that the largest banks have historically found most accommodating; the public's stake is whether oversight of systemically important banks gets stronger or weaker.

industries.industry: Federal Reserve, FDIC, and state bank regulators (as supervisors)
industries.note: The bill strips the Fed and FDIC of supervisory authority over the biggest state-chartered banks and ends state regulators' role entirely [S2][S3]. That loss of independent oversight is a cost to the public as well, since fewer sets of eyes would watch the same institutions.
